output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) supersedes the 2017 criteria: it adds the optic nerve region and the kFLC index, and four or five involved regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time. Optic neuritis is a common first presentation of MS.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Four non-enhancing ovoid periventricular lesions, a left parietal juxtacortical lesion and a dorsal pontine lesion, with a 10 mm enhancing, swollen intraorbital left optic nerve segment; no white matter lesion enhances.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with gadolinium on an MS protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Severe painful left optic neuritis with an earlier hemibody sensory episode: the brain scan shows whether lesions in MS-typical regions are already present and characterises the optic nerve lesion (length, perineural enhancement) that separates MS from MOGAD.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Short non-enhancing right dorsolateral C5-C6 lesion (about 1.2 segments, under half the cross-section); thoracic cord normal; no longitudinally extensive lesion.
action_criteria.label: Cervical and thoracic spinal cord MRI with gadolinium
action_criteria.rationale: The earlier right arm and trunk tingling points to the cervical cord; the study finds that lesion and excludes the longitudinally extensive myelitis of NMOSD.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, metabolic panel, ESR, CRP, TSH and B12 (398 pg/mL); ANA negative; HIV and RPR non-reactive; vitamin D 21 ng/mL.
action_criteria.label: Mimic-exclusion blood panel (CBC, B12, thyroid, HIV)
action_criteria.rationale: Optic neuritis with white matter lesions needs B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, syphilis, HIV and lupus excluded before attributing it to MS.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay.
action_criteria.label: Serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG by cell-based assay
action_criteria.rationale: Optic neuritis with hand-motion acuity is a red flag for NMOSD and MOGAD; both antibodies must be tested by cell-based assay before an MS diagnosis is made.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (6 cells/uL), five CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands, raised IgG index and kFLC index (38.6).
action_criteria.label: CSF with paired serum for oligoclonal bands or kFLC index
action_criteria.rationale: With lesions in all five regions CSF is not needed to establish MS; it is supportive and excludes infection if the picture is doubted.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Prolonged left P100 latency (147 ms) with reduced amplitude (2.1 uV); right eye normal.
action_criteria.label: Visual evoked potentials

action_criteria.rationale: In the first week of optic neuritis OCT shows swelling or normal layers, not thinning; it gives a baseline for later atrophy.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not label this a clinically isolated syndrome or defer disease-modifying therapy to wait for a second attack: lesions in all five regions and the earlier sensory attack establish MS now
Do not rely on an ELISA AQP4-IgG or MOG-IgG assay: cell-based assays are required
Do not treat the optic neuritis with low-dose oral prednisolone alone (associated with more recurrences in the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial)
Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide or cladribine without confirmed effective contraception — both are teratogenic with prolonged effects
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiating B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF.
Explain the diagnosis as relapsing-remitting MS at this presentation, not a clinically isolated syndrome awaiting a second attack; the right arm and trunk episode 8 months ago was an earlier attack.

Treat the severe optic neuritis (hand-motion acuity) with methylprednisolone IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days (or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days) to speed visual recovery; consider plasma exchange if vision does not improve after steroids.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 8 months, lesions in five regions), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception (she takes a combined oral contraceptive).
Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV, HIV and VZV IgG, a lymphocyte count and liver function, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.
Explain that transient visual worsening after hot showers (Uhthoff phenomenon) is heat-related conduction block, not a new relapse.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role here: she has had no seizure or encephalopathy, and EEG does not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
Head CT adds radiation without answering the question: it cannot show the optic nerve or the demyelinating lesions that MRI characterises.
No cardiac symptom or embolic question in a young woman with optic neuritis; echocardiography does not inform the differential.
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; cardiac monitoring has no role in the diagnostic work-up.
FDG-PET does not distinguish demyelination from its mimics and does not change the diagnosis in this typical presentation.

differential.diagnosis: CNS vasculitis (primary or secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus)

key_clinical_evidence: Current attack: five days of painful left visual loss to hand motions with a 3+ left RAPD, red desaturation, mild disc swelling and a 10 mm enhancing intraorbital left optic nerve segment.
Prior attack: two to three weeks of right arm and right trunk tingling 8 months ago, attributed to stress; the non-enhancing right dorsolateral C5-C6 cord lesion fits it.
DIS: 5 of 5 regions: periventricular (four lesions), juxtacortical (left parietal), infratentorial (dorsal pons), spinal cord (C5-C6), optic nerve (left, on MRI and VEP).
With five regions MS is established without a separate test of DIT; five CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands and a kFLC index of 38.6 are supportive.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, a short optic nerve lesion without perineural enhancement and a short cord lesion: NMOSD and MOGAD unlikely despite the severe visual loss.
Vitamin D 21 ng/mL despite supplementation is a comorbidity, not an explanation for the presentation.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Amara Osei is a 26-year-old right-handed African American woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a five-day history of progressive vision loss in her left eye accompanied by pain behind the eye that worsens with eye movement. She reports that five days ago she began noticing blurring and fogginess in her left visual field while studying on her laptop, which she initially attributed to eye strain and fatigue. By the following morning the vision had worsened considerably, and she noticed that colors appeared washed out, particularly reds, which looked brownish through the left eye. She also developed a dull aching pain behind the left eye that became sharper with lateral and upward gaze movements, rating it a 6 out of 10 at worst. Over the next three days, the vision in her left eye deteriorated to the point where she could only perceive hand motions centrally, prompting her roommates to bring her to the emergency department. She reports that her symptoms seem to worsen after hot showers, with the vision becoming even more blurred for 30 to 60 minutes after exposure to heat. On further directed questioning, she recalls that approximately eight months ago she had a two-to-three week episode of tingling and numbness involving the right side of her trunk and right arm in a hemibody distribution. She saw her university health center at the time and was told the numbness was likely stress-related; it resolved spontaneously without treatment. She did not seek further evaluation. She denies any prior episodes of vision loss, diplopia, weakness, ataxia, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or speech difficulty. She denies recent fevers, weight loss, rash, oral ulcers, joint pains, or other systemic symptoms. She denies recent viral illness or vaccinations. She has no history of foreign travel. She is currently in her second year of her PhD program and had been under increased academic stress over the past several weeks.

Mild left optic disc edema on fundoscopy; right disc normal. Visual fields: full to confrontation on the right; left eye — only gross peripheral motion perception. Pain with left eye movement, rated 6/10 in intensity, worsening on upgaze and adduction. CN III-IV-VI: Extraocular movements full bilaterally without nystagmus. No diplopia. CN V: Facial sensation intact bilaterally. CN VII: Face symmetric. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. CN IX-X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Trapezius and sternocleidomastoid 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline without fasciculations.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Speech fluent without dysarthria or paraphasic errors. Language comprehension and repetition intact. Mood anxious but affect appropriate. Mini-Cog score 5/5.

neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally. Triceps 2+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
